title: Review: Rotation with calculus and vector products; Rotational kinetic energy and rolling; Angular momentum and its conservation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics C: Mechanics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: R06-ap1#t1 term and clue written for the game; R05-ap1#t4 term and clue written for the game; R06-ap1#t2 term and clue written for the game; NEW-rot-calc-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: NEW-rot-calc-1#N.3, NEW-rot-calc-2#N.4, R05-1#N.2, R05-ap1#N.9, R06-1#N.3, R06-ap1#N.10, NEW-rot-calc-1#N.6, NEW-rot-calc-2#N.2, R05-1#N.8b, R06-1#N.6b, R06-ap1#N.5b, NEW-rot-calc-2#N.6. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Angular impulse
items.clue: Area under a graph of torque against time; it has the same sense as the torque.

items.label: Slipping
items.clue: Condition in which a wheel's forward speed does not equal rω, so the surfaces slide.

items.label: Angular momentum
items.clue: Quantity L that is conserved in all interactions: never destroyed, only transferred.

items.label: Right-hand rule
items.clue: Fingers along r, curl them in the direction of F: the thumb then gives the direction of τ.

questions.stem: After its motor is switched off, a flywheel's angular velocity is ω(t) = ω₀e^(−bt), where ω₀ and b are positive constants. Through what angle does the flywheel turn between t = 0 and t = 1/b?

A wheel of rotational inertia I starts from rest. The net torque exerted on it depends on its angular position θ as τ = τ₀(1 − θ²/θ₁²), where τ₀ and θ₁ are positive constants, so the torque falls to zero at θ = θ₁. What is the wheel's angular speed at θ = θ₁?

A uniform grinding wheel spins at constant angular velocity on a fixed axle, so its centre of mass stays at rest. A student claims: "The velocities of points on opposite sides of the wheel are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel, and the wheel has no kinetic energy." Which response to the student's claim is correct?

options.text: It is right: the kinetic energies of points moving in opposite directions cancel.
It is right: a wheel whose centre of mass is at rest has no kinetic energy.
It is wrong: each moving point has positive kinetic energy, so the energies add.
It is wrong: the wheel's kinetic energy is (1/2)Mv², where v is its rim speed.

questions.stem: A hoop is spun about its axle and then set down upright on a rough, level floor, with its centre at rest. At first the hoop skids, spinning in place; then it moves off and soon rolls without slipping. What happens to the hoop's total kinetic energy while it skids?

options.text: It stays the same: the rotational KE simply becomes translational KE.
It decreases: the rim slides on the floor, so friction dissipates energy.
It increases: friction pushes the hoop forward, doing positive work on it.
It stays the same: friction on a turning object does no work.

questions.explanation: While v_cm ≠ rω the contact point slides over the floor. Kinetic friction at a sliding contact turns kinetic energy into thermal energy until rolling begins.

questions.stem: A thin hoop (I = MR²) and a uniform solid disc (I = ½MR²) have the same mass M and the same radius R. The hoop rotates about its central axis at angular speed ω; the disc rotates about its central axis at 2ω. How do their angular momenta compare?

options.text: The hoop's is greater, since all of its mass is at the rim.
The disc's is greater, since it spins twice as fast.
They are equal: each is MR²ω.
The disc's is four times the hoop's, since L depends on ω².

questions.explanation: Hoop: MR² × ω. Disc: ½MR² × 2ω = MR²ω. Equal.

questions.stem: An astronaut floats inside a space station, touching nothing and holding nothing, and rotates slowly about an axis through her center of mass. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following could change her angular momentum about that axis?

options.text: Pulling her arms and legs in close to her body
Twisting her torso one way and her legs the other
Pushing sideways on a handrail fixed to the station
Waiting, since spinning slowly dies away when nothing acts

questions.stem: A revolving door, rotational inertia 40 kg m², is at rest. A person pushes on it with a torque that grows steadily: τ = (12 N m s⁻¹)t. Friction is negligible. What is the door's angular velocity at t = 2.0 s?

A small ball of mass m moves at constant speed v in a horizontal circle of radius r at the end of a string. A student claims that the ball's angular momentum about the center of the circle has magnitude mvr, whether it is found from L = Iω or from L = r × p. Which reasoning correctly supports the claim?

options.text: The magnitude of r × p is rp, whatever the angle, and Iω reduces to the same product.
For a point mass, I is mr² and ω is v/r, and v is tangent, perpendicular to r.
Angular momentum is the linear momentum mv, changed into rotational units by multiplying it by r.
The tension along the string exerts a torque about the center that keeps L equal to mvr.

questions.stem: A thin-walled hollow ball (I = (2/3)MR²) is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a ramp. Its centre of mass descends a vertical height of 1.2 m. Use g = 10 m s⁻². What is the speed of its centre of mass at the bottom?

Counterclockwise is taken as positive. A motorized turntable with rotational inertia I is rotating counterclockwise with angular speed ω₀. The motor then brings it to rotate clockwise with angular speed 3ω₀. Using this sign convention for both the initial and final angular momenta, which expression gives the change in the turntable's angular momentum?

A resistive torque slows a spinning wheel so that its angular momentum about its axle decreases with time as L = L₀e^(−t/T), where L₀ and T are positive constants and e is the base of natural logarithms. What is the magnitude of the net torque exerted on the wheel at t = T?

A ball of mass m is thrown horizontally with speed v₀ from point P at the top of a cliff. Air resistance is negligible, and g is the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity. What is the magnitude of the ball's angular momentum about P at time t after it is thrown, before it lands?
